$schema-note: Hand-maintained. Data, not code: nothing under src/ imports this file.
purpose: The guard ledger for WIN-258 TRANCHE 5 — `jobs`' canonical store, the
THIRTEENTH owner behind the one PostgreSQL client ADR M0.3 §15 gives the ORM.
One entry per guard: per scope predicate, per vocabulary check that stands
where no enum stands, per shape check that stands where a migration-only
CHECK stands, per envelope decision that keeps a row an older binary wrote
readable, and per statement the port's contract says must be one statement.
Each carries the file it lives in, the EXACT text that implements it
(`from`), the edit that removes it (`to`), and the NAMED cases that were seen
to go red (`kills`).
IT IS A THIRTEENTH FILE beside mutations.json and the eleven others rather
than an extension of any of them, for the reason the fourth was: thirteen
tranches are thirteen separate claims about thirteen separate port surfaces,
and a reader checking one should not have to read past the other twelve. All
are hashed by the same packages.adapters.config rule and counted together by
the v1 ledger.
WHY THIS TRANCHE NEEDED ITS OWN SWEEP. TEN of `Approval`'s twenty fields have
NO COLUMN. `AgentApproval` predates the model this context extracted, so the
live system put the business `approvalId`, the `source`, who asked, the dedupe
digest, the MCP token, the consumption instant and the human's edits inside the
`arguments` JSON under `__platosApproval`. That is a WIRE FORMAT — rows
carrying it are in the database now — and an envelope that stopped
discriminating would read a legacy row's own arguments as its metadata, or
discard them. Neither is visible in a returned value on a store with one
caller.
AND TWO COLUMNS CARRY VOCABULARIES THE DATABASE DOES NOT HOLD. `Job.status` is
the FIVE-member `WorkStatus` enum of which a `Job` row only ever takes two, and
`Job.invocationType` is a plain TEXT column whose closed set lives only in
`domain/invocation.ts`. A store that CAST either would put a value outside its
union into `assertDispatchable` or `authorizeInvocation`, whose tables are keyed
BY the union — and an unknown invocation type would then authorize nothing
while reporting no error at all.
M-J15 IS THE ONE ENTRY PROVEN IN THE PURE SUITE ALONE, and that is a vocabulary
boundary rather than a weaker claim. The invocation type's COLUMN carries the
pre-cutover vendor name behind an `@map`; `domain/invocation.ts` deliberately
does not spell it and `scripts/vocabulary-boundary.mjs` will not have this
package spell it either, so a container suite could not plant such a row without
naming it. `jobs-rows.test.ts` hands the value straight to the reader instead.
AND ONE COLUMN'S CONSTRAINT IS WHY THE OUTCOME RIDES IN AN ENVELOPE OF ITS OWN.
`AgentApproval_resolution_json_root` admits an OBJECT or SQL NULL, and
`Approval.outcome` is `JsonValue | null` — so an array, a string and a number
are all values the port admits and the column refuses. The live
`markMcpConsumed` wrapped a non-object as `{ value: x }`, which is
indistinguishable on read from an outcome that IS `{ value: x }`. M-J27, M-J28
and M-J29 are the three halves of that guard.
procedure: PROVE THE SUITES GREEN FIRST. Tranche 1's first sweep reported 22 kills and
every one was VACUOUS: a context's `dist` had been cleaned, so every suite
failed to load its import and would have 'died' against any mutation at all,
including none. The driver runs each suite set UNMUTATED and refuses to sweep
unless it is green with a non-zero executed case count, and classifies a run
with no executed cases as VACUOUS rather than as a kill.
THE INTEGRATION SUITES RUN ON A REAL POSTGRESQL, in a container, on the machine
that has a daemon. `jobs-rows.test.ts` is the only suite here that runs without
one, and it is the one that reaches the mapping branches a container suite
cannot: a container only ever reads rows THIS binary wrote, so the
legacy-envelope and unknown-vocabulary branches are unreachable from it except
through the rows `jobs-rules.integration.test.ts` plants as raw SQL.
EVERY `from` IS A UNIQUE SUBSTRING OF ITS FILE and is applied literally, so a
sweep that silently matched nothing is impossible: the driver refuses an entry
whose `from` occurs zero times or more than once.
RESULT, 2026-09-06, against PostgreSQL 16 in a container: 75 entries, 75
KILLED, 0 SURVIVED, 0 VACUOUS. Every baseline suite set was green with a
non-zero executed case count before its mutation was applied, and every `from`
matched its file exactly once.
THE FIRST SWEEP'S SURVIVORS ARE WHY SIX CASES EXIST. The dedupe lookup's three
predicates were measured through a scenario in which every row was pending and
every row was an `mcp_tool_call`, so removing either predicate changed nothing;
the listing's DEFAULT thirty-day window is a question the in-memory double
cannot be asked at all, because it applies no date filter; the platform-wide
enumeration's `distinct` and its pending filter were measured against one scope
holding one row; the writes were never aimed at another tenant's row; and the
erasure's tenant narrowing was measured where only one environment held a row.
Each is now a named case in `jobs-isolation.integration.test.ts` rather than a
widened entry.
TWO ENTRIES WERE WITHDRAWN RATHER THAN CARRIED. A mutation of
`readApprovalOutcome`'s non-object branch is unfalsifiable, because
`AgentApproval_resolution_json_root` means no row can hold a non-object there;
and a mutation of the same function's null branch answers null either way. An
entry nothing can kill is not a guard, and listing one would make this ledger
say something it cannot support.

kills: the fakes and the real store answer the same scenario identically

mutations.name: M-J66 approvals: findPending returns only pending rows
mutations.from:
where: { ...scopedWhere(scope), status: "PENDING" },
          select: APPROVAL_COLUMNS,
          orderBy: [{ createdAt: "asc" }, { id: "asc" }],
mutations.to:
where: { ...scopedWhere(scope) },
          select: APPROVAL_COLUMNS,
          orderBy: [{ createdAt: "asc" }, { id: "asc" }],
mutations.note: The sweep judges what it is handed. A decided approval in that list would be flipped to `timed_out` over a decision a human already made.
kills: the fakes and the real store answer the same scenario identically

mutations.name: M-J67 approvals: the platform-wide enumeration is pending-only
mutations.note: A scope whose approvals are all decided has nothing for a sweep to do, and visiting it is work the sweep pays for on every install.
kills: a scope is enumerated ONCE while it holds a pending row, and not at all after

mutations.name: M-J68 approvals: the platform-wide enumeration is DISTINCT
mutations.note: Without it the sweep visits an environment once per waiting approval, which is the N+1 the port split the enumeration from the sweep to prevent.
kills: a scope is enumerated ONCE while it holds a pending row, and not at all after

mutations.name: M-J69 approvals: the page window is checked before the statement
mutations.note: A negative `take` is read by PostgreSQL as "page backwards from the offset", which is a different page rather than an error.
kills: a page window the double accepts and PostgreSQL reads backwards is refused

mutations.name: M-J70 approvals: resolve guards the approval it is handed
mutations.to:
const client = transactions.writer(transaction);
        // THE GUARD IS `status: "PENDING"` IN THE `where`
mutations.note: `resolve` is the one write that carries a human's edits, and the edit shape the envelope cannot hold is refused here or lost silently.
kills: an edit whose editedArguments is JSON null is refused rather than silently lost

mutations.name: M-J71 erasure: a subject-less selector matches nothing
mutations.from:
const principalId = selector.principalId;
  if (principalId === null) return null;
mutations.to:
const principalId = selector.principalId;
  if (false) return null;
mutations.note: A null subject would make the `WHERE` a tenant alone — every approval of every person in that organization. `selectorFor` answers null for an `entity` subject, so this is reachable from the erasure target itself.
kills: the fakes and the real store answer the same scenario identically

mutations.name: M-J72 erasure: the operator who DECIDED is a subject too
mutations.from:
{ respondedBy: principalId },
      { arguments: { path: [APPROVAL_METADATA_MARKER, "requestedBy"], equals: principalId } },
mutations.note: `respondedBy` names a human who authorised a specific action with specific arguments. An erasure that missed it would leave that name behind.
kills: the fakes and the real store answer the same scenario identically

mutations.name: M-J73 erasure: the requester in the envelope is a subject too
mutations.note: The requester has no COLUMN, so a store that matched only the column would erase the deciders and leave every asker.
kills: the fakes and the real store answer the same scenario identically

mutations.name: M-J74 erasure: the selector is narrowed by its tenant scope
mutations.note: An erasure addressed at one environment would reach every environment in the install that holds a row for that subject.
kills: one subject with approvals in two environments is counted per environment

mutations.name: M-J75 erasure: a subject-less erasure destroys nothing
mutations.from:
if (where === null) return ok(0);
        const client = transactions.writer(transaction);
mutations.to:
if (where === null) return ok(1);
        const client = transactions.writer(transaction);
mutations.note: The fail-CLOSED direction: it answers zero and destroys nothing rather than matching broadly, and the receipt must say zero rather than claim a row.
kills: the fakes and the real store answer the same scenario identically

mutations.name: M-J76 erasure: the receipt reports what the delete destroyed
mutations.from:
const destroyed = await client.agentApproval.deleteMany({ where });
        return ok(destroyed.count);
mutations.note: Nothing holds a foreign key TO an approval, so this single count IS the receipt and there is no cascade to recover it from.
kills: the fakes and the real store answer the same scenario identically
